readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 17:1-19:21. These are the great chapters about Elijah: the drought, the widow of Zarephath, the showdown on Mount Carmel, and the quiet voice on Mount Horeb. Read them slowly, and pay attention to what God does at each stage.
settingTheScene: Under Ahab and Jezebel, Baal worship has been established as the official religion in Israel. Baal was a Canaanite storm and fertility god, credited with sending rain. Into this setting steps Elijah the Tishbite, a prophet from Gilead. His name means “my God is Yahweh.” He announces a drought, and the confrontation is on: which God controls the rain?
observation: “As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word” (17:1).
The LORD sends Elijah to the brook Cherith, where ravens bring him bread and meat (17:2-6).
At Zarephath, a widow gives Elijah her last meal, and “the jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty” (17:8-16).
Elijah raises the widow’s son, and she says, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth” (17:17-24).
“How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (18:21).
Baal’s prophets cry out from morning to evening, but “there was no voice. No one answered” (18:26-29).
“Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering”; the people said, “The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God” (18:38-39).
At Horeb, God is not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but in “a low whisper” (19:11-12).
interpretation:
The drought is a direct challenge to Baal. The god of the storm cannot bring rain, and the LORD controls the weather. But the first part of Elijah’s ministry takes place away from the public eye. He hides at Cherith, fed by ravens, and then goes to Zarephath, in Sidon, the homeland of Jezebel. The God of Israel is caring for a foreign widow and her son, and showing that his power reaches beyond Israel. Jesus will point to this very story (Luke 4:25-26).

The showdown at Carmel is the center of the passage. Elijah does not ask the people for loyalty to God alone. He asks them to decide: “How long will you go limping between two opinions?” Divided loyalty is not neutrality. It is a form of unfaithfulness. The contest is simple. The god who answers by fire is God. Baal’s prophets cry and cut themselves all day. Nothing happens. Elijah mocks them, “Cry aloud, for he is a god.” Then he rebuilds the LORD’s altar with twelve stones, representing all Israel, soaks it with water three times, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls. The people declare, “The LORD, he is God.”

Then comes an odd turn. After the greatest victory of his life, Elijah runs in fear from Jezebel’s threat. He sits under a broom tree and asks to die. “It is enough; now, O LORD, take my life.” The prophet who stood boldly on Carmel is now exhausted, depressed, and alone. God’s response is gentle. He lets Elijah sleep and sends an angel with food. The first thing God offers is rest and a meal.

At Horeb, the same mountain where Moses met God, Elijah expects power. Wind, earthquake, and fire pass, but the LORD is not in them. Then a low whisper. The God of fire is also the God of the quiet voice. And he tells Elijah that he is not alone: seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal. He gives him work to do, including calling Elisha.
connection: Jesus cited the widow of Zarephath in his first sermon (Luke 4:25-26). John the Baptist came “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17), and Jesus said Elijah had already come (Matthew 17:11-13). Jesus fed the five thousand, a greater miracle of provision. He raised a widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:11-17). At the transfiguration, Elijah appeared with Moses to speak with Jesus (Luke 9:30). Romans 11:2-5 uses the story of the seven thousand to show that God always keeps a remnant.
application:
Where are you limping between two opinions? Make your decision today.

If you are exhausted after a hard season, remember that God first gave Elijah food and sleep.

Listen for the low whisper of God in the quiet today.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from limping between two opinions.
Tell him where you are weary, and ask him to feed and rest you.
Listen for his whisper and tell him what you hear.
